tldr: The authors propose Res-HIL, a framework that freezes an imitation model pretrained on a small number of demonstrations and efficiently learns a residual policy from real-time human interventions by extracting two learning signals: direct residual supervision and penalty on preceding autonomous behavior. On a real robot, with only 20 demonstrations and 10 minutes of online training, it outperforms pure imitation learning trained on 100 demonstrations.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of Res-HIL. The outputs of a frozen base policy (pretrained ACT) and an actively learning residual policy are summed to drive the robot, while a human intervenes whenever failure is imminent. Human teleoperation provides a direct supervision signal (BC) for the residual policy and also acts as reward shaping that penalizes autonomous actions immediately prior to intervention, achieving efficient off-policy learning.
overview:
Imitation Learning (IL) is a standard approach for teaching complex behaviors to robots, but it constantly suffers from the "distribution shift" problem, where performance rapidly degrades once the robot enters states not covered by demonstrations. Collecting massive amounts of additional demonstrations to cover failures requires substantial human effort, while retraining or fine-tuning the entire model from scratch via online reinforcement learning (RL) leads to difficult exploration, particularly in long-horizon tasks.

To address this, the authors turned to residual reinforcement learning, built around the idea that one can simply keep the original imitation model frozen and add only the missing corrections (residuals) through RL. Furthermore, they combined it with a Human-in-the-Loop (HIL) mechanism where a human intervenes via teleoperation when the robot is about to fail. The true strength of Res-HIL lies in treating human intervention not merely as a safety net, but converting it into two complementary learning signals: a direct imitation target (BC loss) for the residual, and reward shaping to preemptively penalize actions leading to failure.

Evaluating across five tasks on a real UR5 arm, including high-precision peg-in-hole insertion and a long-horizon task routing a cable around obstacles, Res-HIL started from an initial model trained on only 20 demonstrations and outperformed existing HIL-RL and autonomous residual RL after just 10 minutes of online training. Ultimately, it not only significantly improved upon the original imitation model, but also surpassed a pure imitation model trained with five times more demonstrations (100 demonstrations) in terms of higher success rates and shorter execution times.
contributions: Proposal of Res-HIL, a human-in-the-loop residual reinforcement learning framework that freezes a pretrained imitation policy and leverages human interventions to efficiently learn corrective residual actions

Design of a mechanism that utilizes human interventions as two complementary learning signals: direct supervision on the residual policy (BC loss) and a penalty on autonomous actions preceding intervention (reward shaping)
Introduction of zero initialization for the residual policy output layer, preventing behavioral collapse early in training and stabilizing as well as accelerating online learning

Demonstration across five real-robot tasks involving contact-rich precision and long-horizon cable routing, showing that with only 20 demonstrations and short online training, Res-HIL outperforms baselines and imitation models trained on large demonstration sets

sections.heading: Why Imitation Learning Alone Falls Short and Why Human Intervention Meets Residual Learning
sections.summary: While imitation learning is effective, small error accumulations often lead to unrecoverable states, and collecting additional demonstrations has practical limits. On the other hand, human-in-the-loop RL (HIL-RL) trains full-task policies and requires massive time for long-horizon tasks, while standard residual RL suffers from inefficient autonomous exploration on real robots. This work combines them into Res-HIL, extracting two complementary learning signals from interventions.
sections.details:
When robots perform complex manipulation on behalf of humans, imitation learning from human demonstrations (especially Behavior Cloning: BC) is very popular. However, policies trained with BC suffer from compounding errors once they drift outside the demonstration distribution, making recovery impossible. This is particularly fatal in contact-rich or long-horizon tasks. Collecting additional demonstrations can mitigate this, but human effort scales substantially.

Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning (HIL-RL) has gained attention as an alternative, where a human intervenes during robot execution to steer it back to correct trajectories. However, existing HIL-RL methods (such as HIL-SERL) learn the complete task policy online from scratch or fine-tune the entire model, causing required robot run time and human commitment to soar as tasks become longer.

Another approach is residual reinforcement learning (Residual RL), which adds corrective actions on top of a pretrained model. Its strength lies in leveraging base knowledge, but it relies on autonomous trial-and-error exploration to discover corrections, which can be dangerous or inefficient in real-robot manipulation.

The key insight here is that these two paradigms complement each other's weaknesses. Res-HIL keeps the pretrained imitation policy frozen and trains only a residual policy. Furthermore, it uses human intervention data as direct supervision for the residual, and turns the timing of interventions into reward penalties for preceding actions. This enables targeted, safe, and rapid correction of failure points without destroying the capabilities of the base policy.

sections.heading: The Intersection of Human-in-the-Loop RL and Residual Reinforcement Learning
sections.summary: Most HIL-RL methods focus on updating the full policy, whereas prior residual RL methods struggle with inefficient autonomous exploration. Even compared to recent intervention-guided residual RL methods, Res-HIL distinguishes itself clearly by eliminating the need for auxiliary reward models, calculating residual targets directly from human inputs for BC loss, and applying reward penalties.
sections.details:
Related work can be divided broadly into three categories.

### II-A Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning (HIL-RL)
Methods where humans intervene upon detecting danger or stagnation include Intervention-aided RL for navigation and HIL-SERL for training visuomotor policies directly on real manipulation robots. Recent extensions include fine-tuning VLA models (ConRFT) and industrial assembly (SHaRe-RL). Other approaches filter out actions immediately prior to intervention as low quality (Sirius) or convert them into preference models (PACT). However, these optimize the full task policy rather than operating in a "frozen imitation policy + residual correction" framework like Res-HIL.

### II-B Residual Reinforcement Learning (Residual RL)
This paradigm adds corrective actions on top of base controllers or imitation policies. Starting from adding residuals to traditional feedback controllers, recent works include ResiP combining residuals with BC policies, Policy Decorator refining large imitation models, and ResFiT scaling to high-DoF arms by reusing demonstration data. However, these still rely on autonomous exploration, making it extremely difficult to discover corrective actions once the robot enters states it cannot recover from autonomously.

### II-C Residual Reinforcement Learning with Human Guidance
Very recently, attempts have emerged to integrate human intervention into residual RL. For instance, FTC incorporates visual affordance reward models, whereas Res-HIL requires no such auxiliary models. HiL-ResRL puts human residual inputs directly into a replay buffer for SAC training, whereas Res-HIL explicitly constructs a residual target from the difference between the full human action and the base policy action, learning it directly via BC loss. Using the occurrence of interventions as an indicator of imminent failure for reward shaping also marks a major distinction from prior work.

sections.heading: How Res-HIL Works: Extracting Two Learning Signals from Interventions to Safely Train Residuals
sections.summary: A pretrained imitation policy is frozen, and its output is summed with a TD3-based residual policy to control the robot. When a human intervenes, the residual target is computed from the full action to supervise the policy directly via BC loss, while an exponentially decaying penalty is applied to preceding autonomous transitions via reward shaping. Initializing the output layer to zero prevents early behavioral collapse.
sections.details:
Here is how the algorithm and design of Res-HIL work.

### III-A Problem Formulation and Action Composition
Given an observation $o_t$ from the environment (camera images and proprioception), we have a base policy $\pi_{\mathrm{BC}}$ pretrained on demonstrations with frozen parameters, and a residual policy $\pi_{\theta}$ to be learned. The action $\boldsymbol{a}_t$ actually sent to the robot is simply the sum of both:
$$\boldsymbol{a}_t = \pi_{\mathrm{BC}}(o_t) + \pi_{\theta}(o_t)$$
To optimize the residual policy, Res-HIL adopts TD3, an off-policy RL algorithm that operates stably in continuous action spaces.

### III-B Human Intervention and Buffer Management
Whenever an operator decides that failure or damage to the robot or parts is imminent, they intervene via teleoperation (a 3D mouse), fully overriding control with human action $\boldsymbol{a}^{\mathrm{human}}_t$. Once recovered, control is released back to autonomous execution. Data is split into $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{online}}$, which stores all transitions, and $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{offline}}$, which stores initial demonstrations and intervention transitions. Training batches are sampled 50/50 from both buffers. This prevents infrequent but critical human corrections from being drowned out during learning.

### III-C Zero Initialization of the Residual Policy
If the residual policy outputs random actions at the start of training, it immediately disrupts the pretrained behavior of the base policy. Res-HIL initializes the weights and biases of the residual policy's final output layer to zero. Consequently, the initial residual output is strictly zero, allowing training to start smoothly directly from the base policy's behavior.

### III-D Intervention-Aware Reward Shaping
Under sparse rewards given only upon task completion, the agent cannot tell what went wrong when it fails midway. Res-HIL applies an exponentially decaying penalty to autonomous transitions up to $I$ steps prior to the intervention start:
$$\tilde{r}_t = r_t - \lambda_{\mathrm{int}} \rho^{I - (k - t)}$$
Actions closer to the intervention receive a heavier penalty, while earlier actions receive lighter penalties. To prevent excessive penalties from negating the task success reward during frequent interventions, the penalty is applied only to the first $K$ intervention segments within an episode.

### III-E Optimization Objectives
The Critic (Q-function) is updated via the standard Bellman error in TD3. The loss for the residual Actor includes two additional terms alongside the TD3 Q-value maximization: a regularization term to prevent unnecessarily large residuals (norm of residual actions), and a Behavior Cloning (BC) loss on human intervention data. Given the full human action $\boldsymbol{a}^{\mathrm{human}}_t$, the residual target label is defined as $\boldsymbol{a}^{\mathrm{target}}_{\mathrm{res}, t} = \boldsymbol{a}^{\mathrm{human}}_t - \pi_{\mathrm{BC}}(o_t)$, and MSE (mean squared error) is minimized. This BC loss allows human corrective motions to be instantly baked into the residual policy without waiting for slow RL exploration.

captions.F2: Detailed interaction and training loops of Res-HIL. The sum of the frozen Base Policy and learning Residual Policy is sent to the robot, with Human Action taking priority during interventions. Intervention data is stored in the Intervention Buffer, preceding autonomous actions are penalized via Reward Shaping, and both Critic and Residual Actor are updated simultaneously.

sections.heading: Validation on Five Contact-Rich and Long-Horizon Real-Robot Manipulation Tasks
sections.summary: Using a UR5 arm with two or three cameras, experiments were conducted on five tasks: peg-in-hole (Easy/Hard) with tight tolerances, long-horizon cable routing and insertion (2 cameras/3 cameras), and vent insertion with strict ordering. Comparisons were made against the standalone base policy (ACT), autonomous residual RL (ResFiT), and baseline HIL-RL (HIL-SERL).
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted on a real UR5 robot arm using images from two wrist-mounted cameras, proprioception, and, for some tasks, an external side camera viewing the whole scene. Features were extracted using a pretrained ResNet-10, controlling the end-effector in relative Cartesian coordinates (translation and rotation).

### IV-A Evaluation Tasks
Five contact-rich, challenging manipulation tasks were evaluated:
- **Peg-in-hole (Easy / Hard)**: High-precision insertion. Easy randomizes peg orientation up to 15 degrees. Hard randomizes peg orientation up to 25 degrees and gripper tilt up to 10 degrees along two orthogonal axes.
- **Cable routing and insertion (2 cameras / 3 cameras)**: A long-horizon task where a grasped cable is routed behind a cylindrical obstacle and its connector is then inserted into a socket. The 2-camera version uses only wrist cameras where the obstacle is occluded, while the 3-camera version adds an external camera capturing the obstacle continuously.
- **Vent insertion**: Inserting a vent cover in a designated orientation and sequence (inserting one edge first, then pressing the opposite side). Forcing it straight down or inserting in reverse risks damaging the component and is counted as a failure.

The training time budget was set strictly: 20 minutes for Easy peg insertion and 45 minutes for the other four tasks.

### IV-B Baselines and Initial Conditions
Baselines included ACT (frozen imitation model trained only on initial demonstrations), ResFiT (autonomous residual RL without human guidance), HIL-SERL (a representative HIL-RL method fine-tuning the full policy), and Naive Res-HIL (Res-HIL without zero initialization, reward shaping, and BC loss). Conditions using 100 demonstrations were also tested for ACT and ResFiT, but all online learning methods were initialized with only 20 demonstrations.

captions.F1: Experimental setup for the long-horizon "Cable routing and insertion" task. The robot must route the grasped USB cable around a cylindrical obstacle (1) and insert its connector into a socket (2). Both stages must be executed sequentially, presenting an extremely large exploration space.

sections.heading: A Decisive Gap After 10 Minutes: Outperforming Imitation Learning Trained on 100 Demonstrations
sections.summary: Res-HIL achieved the highest success rate across all five tasks after just 10 minutes of training, reaching 100% on three tasks and over 88% on all tasks upon completion. While HIL-SERL failed on the long-horizon cable routing task, Res-HIL showed strong adaptability and completed tasks with high precision in shorter execution times (5.46s on average) than ACT trained on 100 demonstrations.
sections.details:
Key takeaways from the experimental results:

### V-A Task Success Rates and Learning Speed
After just 10 minutes of online training, Res-HIL achieved a 100% success rate on Easy peg-in-hole and 92% on 3-camera cable routing, outperforming all baselines on all five tasks. In contrast, HIL-SERL lagged significantly behind at 10 minutes, while ResFiT and Naive Res-HIL had near-zero success rates.

In final success rates at the end of training, Res-HIL reached between 88% and 100% across all tasks. This was especially evident in the long-horizon cable routing task: HIL-SERL failed to solve the exploration challenge of the full policy, resulting in a 0% success rate, whereas Res-HIL achieved 88% (2 cameras) and 100% (3 cameras). This dramatically improved upon the base policy (20-demo ACT) alone, which scored 46% and 70%, respectively. Remarkably, it even surpassed ACT pretrained with five times more demonstrations (100 demos), which achieved 72% with 2 cameras and 90% with 3 cameras.

### V-B Execution Time (Cycle Time) Comparison
Comparing the average completion time on successful episodes, Res-HIL averaged 5.46 seconds across all tasks. This was faster than 100-demo ACT (5.83 seconds) and 20-demo ACT (7.73 seconds). Learning corrective actions eliminated hesitation, enabling smoother and faster motions.

### V-C Human Intervention Efficiency and Ablation Study
Human intervention rates dropped sharply as training progressed, reaching near-zero once the policy converged. Total human intervention time prior to convergence was lower than that of HIL-SERL, achieving rapid adaptation with minimal human burden.

Ablation experiments on Easy peg-in-hole highlighted the role of each component:
- **Removing zero initialization**: Doubled convergence time from 8 minutes to 16 minutes due to erratic early behavior.
- **Removing reward shaping**: Failed to converge within 30 minutes, capping success at 92% and requiring persistent human intervention throughout.
- **Removing BC loss**: Success rate plummeted to just 20%.
These results show that direct residual supervision via BC loss is critical for performance, while reward shaping underpins training efficiency.

sections.heading: Connecting Pretrained Knowledge and Human Intuition Without Waste
sections.summary: Res-HIL effectively bridges the stability of pretrained policies and the adaptability of human intervention within a residual learning framework. It demonstrates successful real-robot learning for long-horizon, high-precision manipulation with minimal demonstrations and human intervention time. Future work will explore scaling to broader task varieties and further reducing human effort.
sections.details:
When automating robot tasks in the real world, both solving everything from scratch via RL and relying purely on collecting massive demonstration sets face practical limits. Res-HIL offers a practical and rational alternative: build a rough base policy from a small number of demonstrations, and let human intervention quickly teach the missing corrections as residuals.

The core strength of this paper is treating valuable human intervention data not just as a trajectory reset, but fully extracting two learning signals: residual imitation data and a penalty on actions preceding failure. This enabled flawless execution on long-horizon tasks (such as cable routing), which have historically challenged online RL, in just tens of minutes of real-robot training.

Future research will likely focus on scaling to more diverse and complex tasks while driving the required human intervention effort closer to zero.

takeaways: Combining imitation learning from small demonstration sets with human-guided residual RL yields superior sample efficiency in long-horizon, high-precision real-robot manipulation

Rather than simply storing human interventions in a replay buffer, converting them into direct residual targets (BC loss) and decaying penalties on preceding actions (reward shaping) maximizes learning signals
Zero-initializing the residual network's output layer prevents degradation of the base policy at the start of training and significantly accelerates convergence

With only 20 initial demonstrations and 10 to 45 minutes of online intervention training, Res-HIL outperforms pure imitation models trained on five times more demonstrations (100 demos) in both success rate and cycle time
limitations: Requires a human operator to monitor the robot in real time and intervene with a 3D mouse, keeping the operator committed during training time
Direct real-robot comparisons with concurrently published related methods (such as FTC and HiL-ResRL) were not conducted due to submission timelines
Requires tuning task-dependent parameters such as intervention release timing and the reward penalty coefficient ($\lambda_{\mathrm{int}}$)
